values.label: Disabled automatic garbage collection
values.description: Automatic foreground garbage collection is disabled so cleanup is delegated to background maintenance.

values.label: User-controlled maintenance suspension
values.description: Allowing users to pause or unregister automatic client maintenance.

selected_clusters.name: Client Pack Rewrite Strategy
selected_clusters.description: Which pack-rewrite strategy controls client repository storage and pack growth?

values.label: Incremental pack-file repacking
values.description: Rewrite manageable batches of packs incrementally instead of rewriting all repository data at once.

values.label: Single-pack full repacking
values.description: Rewrite all repository data into one packfile in a single conventional repack operation.

values.label: Pack-count and storage reduction
values.description: Reduce pack counts and repository storage footprint through incremental maintenance.

values.label: File-handle pressure from unbounded pack growth
values.description: Unbounded pack accumulation creates file-handle scalability pressure during Git operations.

selected_clusters.name: Client Pack Indexing and Compression
selected_clusters.description: Which indexing and compression mechanisms reduce client pack access or storage costs?

values.label: Multi-pack-index maintenance
values.description: Maintain an index spanning multiple packs and use it to coordinate pack replacement and lookup.

values.label: Pack-file delta compression
values.description: Store Git objects in delta-compressed packfiles for space-efficient repository storage.

selected_clusters.name: Client Object-Cleanup Pipeline
selected_clusters.description: Which object types and storage structures are cleaned or rewritten during client repository maintenance?

values.label: Loose-object cleanup
values.description: Remove accumulated loose-object overhead during repository maintenance.

values.label: Two-phase repack and pack expiration
values.description: Create replacement packs and redirect references before deleting unreferenced old packs.

selected_clusters.name: Replica Compaction Strategy
selected_clusters.description: How are compacted repository representations produced and made available to replicas?

values.label: Primary-only repository compaction
values.description: Compact repositories on the primary and propagate the resulting compaction to replicas.

values.label: Replica-side repository repacking
values.description: Independently repack repository copies on replicas rather than consuming propagated compacted output.

values.label: S3-distributed compacted packs
values.description: Distribute already-compacted packfiles through S3 so replicas avoid local repacking.

values.label: Loose-object storage overhead
values.description: Accumulated loose objects increase disk usage and impair repository performance.

selected_clusters.name: Client Commit-Graph Maintenance
selected_clusters.description: How commit-graph data is generated and validated during client repository maintenance.

values.label: Commit-graph generation maintenance
values.description: Generating commit-graph files during background repository maintenance for large-repository performance.

values.label: Commit-graph verification
values.description: Verifying generated commit-graph data as part of repository maintenance.

selected_clusters.name: Client Repository Setup
selected_clusters.description: How existing repositories are registered and configured for large-repository client operation.

values.label: Existing-repository registration workflow
values.description: Enabling client performance management by registering an existing repository.

values.label: Local Git configuration setup
values.description: Applying local Git configuration during client repository registration.

values.label: Background repository configuration updates
values.description: Newly supported client settings are applied asynchronously to registered repositories.

selected_clusters.name: Large-repository data acquisition strategy
selected_clusters.description: Which server-to-client strategy supplies repository objects and history for large-repository operations?

relations.reading: Choices on Large-repository data acquisition strategy limit the options available on Repository Replication Granularity
relations.rationale: Git network transfer requires packfiles, limiting which server-side distribution units can provide efficient cloning and fetching.

relations.reading: Choices on Large-repository data acquisition strategy affect the outcomes of Replica Consistency and Availability Policy
relations.rationale: Protocol reads and cache-server placement determine where repository data must be available and how consistently replicas must serve it.

values.label: Git protocol without GVFS infrastructure
values.description: Repositories lacking suitable GVFS infrastructure use the ordinary Git protocol instead.

values.label: GVFS-protocol cloning
values.description: Use the GVFS protocol for cloning very large repositories when the hosting service supports it.

values.label: Centralized missing-object delivery
values.description: Rely on a central authority to deliver objects absent from clients rather than preserving fully distributed object availability.

selected_clusters.name: Client-side large-repository access implementation
selected_clusters.description: Which client-side mechanism and capability-integration approach presents or manages very large repositories?

values.label: Virtualized filesystem access
values.description: Use a virtualized filesystem layer to present very large repository contents to clients without materializing everything.

values.label: GVFS Protocol in standard Git
values.description: Bring Scalar's service-specific GVFS Protocol support into the standard Git client.

values.label: Virtualized filesystem for object and working-tree access
values.description: Use a virtualized filesystem to defer object and populated-working-tree costs from clients.

selected_clusters.name: Repository Replication Granularity
selected_clusters.description: What unit of repository state is replicated or stored across infrastructure.

relations.reading: Choices on Repository Replication Granularity limit the options available on Replica Consistency and Availability Policy
relations.rationale: Distribution at object, packfile, or repository level changes replication coordination requirements and the consistency surface exposed to clients.

relations.reading: Choices on Repository Replication Granularity affect the outcomes of Durable Repository Write Storage
relations.rationale: The chosen storage representation determines local I/O behavior, compaction needs, and the cost of propagating repository changes.

values.label: Packfile-level replication
values.description: Replication operates on packfiles while preserving Git repositories and avoiding a modified Git implementation.

values.label: Git implementation distribution
values.description: Git itself is distributed or modified as the replication unit for unusual repositories.

values.label: Object-level distributed key-value storage
values.description: Content-addressed objects are mapped individually into a distributed key-value store.

values.label: DHT-backed Git object storage
values.description: A custom Git implementation stores objects through a distributed hash table instead of ordinary packfiles.

values.label: Filesystem block-level replication
values.description: Repository replication operates on filesystem blocks rather than Git application updates.

selected_clusters.name: Git Network Transfer Format
selected_clusters.description: Which Git transfer representation serves repository data between clients and infrastructure.

values.label: Packfile-based Git network transfer
values.description: Git transfers repository data as packfiles regardless of the server-side storage layout.

values.label: Partial clone for demand-driven file transfer
values.description: Only content required by the current checkout is transferred initially.

selected_clusters.name: Replication layer
selected_clusters.description: At which layer is repository state copied between replicas?

relations.reading: Choices on Replication layer affect the outcomes of Replica Consistency and Availability Policy
relations.rationale: Replica allocation, rematerialization, and propagation architecture change replica availability and consistency behavior.

values.label: Git application-level replication
values.description: Repository replication operates on Git application updates rather than filesystem blocks.

values.label: Filesystem-level repository distribution
values.description: Distribute repository storage at the filesystem layer while leaving the application and Git implementation unchanged.

selected_clusters.name: Replica propagation and repair method
selected_clusters.description: How are repository contents propagated, repaired, or rebalanced between repository copies?

values.label: Unsynchronized packfile distribution
values.description: Fan out packfiles without consensus because unreachable objects need not yet be synchronized.

values.label: Git-and-rsync replication stack
values.description: Combining Git and rsync to replicate, repair, and rebalance repository content across file servers.

selected_clusters.name: Repository-serving distribution boundary
selected_clusters.description: What intermediary or communication boundary distributes repository operations across repository-serving infrastructure?

values.label: Proxy-mediated multi-fileserver replication
values.description: A proxy replicates each push across multiple repository fileservers.

values.label: RPC-based remote repository operations
values.description: Access repository storage through RPC so application instances can scale independently of repository-serving machines.

selected_clusters.name: Replica Allocation and Lifecycle
selected_clusters.description: How are repository replicas allocated, retired, reclaimed, and rematerialized across infrastructure?

values.label: Multi-disk and multi-machine repository distribution
values.description: Distributing repositories across many disks and machines to increase parallelism and preserve availability after crashes.

values.label: Remote-fileserver horizontal scalability
values.description: Scale repository-serving capacity by adding remote fileservers behind application-level repository operations.

values.label: Elastic per-repository replica allocation
values.description: Adjust replica counts independently per repository, scaling hot repositories up and relying on durable storage for small repositories.

values.label: Idle-replica garbage collection and rematerialization
values.description: Remove inactive repository replicas from node disks and reconstruct them from durable log state when traffic returns.

selected_clusters.name: Repository Physical Storage
selected_clusters.description: Where and in what native storage form are repository copies physically kept?

values.label: Native Git repository storage
values.description: Replicas retain actual Git repositories so clients receive the native format without transformation.

values.label: Local NVMe repository storage
values.description: Repositories are stored on local NVMe because packfile access requires fast random reads.

values.label: Blob storage for Git packfiles
values.description: Git packfiles are physically stored as objects in blob storage.

values.label: Repository disks as warm caches
values.description: Treat local repository copies as reconstructible caches rather than authoritative repository storage.

values.label: Networked-filesystem repository storage
values.description: Keep repositories on networked filesystems rather than local repository fileservers or object storage.

values.label: Dedicated repository fileservers
values.description: Place repositories on dedicated fileservers accessed remotely by the application.

values.label: Single-machine repository co-location
values.description: Keep application and repository copies together on one physical machine.

values.label: Single-machine repository placement
values.description: Keep each repository copy on one physical machine rather than distributing that repository across multiple machines.

values.label: Git filesystem-semantics mismatch
values.description: Local-filesystem assumptions about locking, tearing, reading, and syncing conflict with networked storage behavior.

values.label: Distributed-filesystem performance and correctness failure
values.description: Distributed filesystem approaches remain slow and unreliable for Git repository access.

selected_clusters.name: Durable Repository Write Storage
selected_clusters.description: How repository writes are durably logged, batched, acknowledged, and materialized in storage.

relations.reading: Choices on Durable Repository Write Storage affect the outcomes of Replica Consistency and Availability Policy
relations.rationale: WAL propagation and replicated compaction establish how replicas receive writes and preserve consistent repository state.

values.label: WAL-first storage architecture
values.description: A write-ahead log provides the basis for horizontal scaling and repository-change propagation.

values.label: S3-backed write-ahead log
values.description: S3 supplies durable WAL updates and determines cluster push-ingest latency.

values.label: S3 Express One Zone
values.description: Lower-latency S3 storage is used to increase push throughput in high-performance clusters.

values.label: One-object-storage-write-per-push
values.description: Issuing an independent object-storage write for every push.

values.label: Batched object-storage writes
values.description: Batching durable object-storage writes so busy repositories avoid one storage operation per push.

values.label: Durability-gated push acknowledgement
values.description: Acknowledging pushes only after their write-ahead-log data is durably persisted.

values.label: WAL-index-gated push publication
values.description: Publishing a push only after local reference preparation and WAL-index recording establish visibility.

values.label: Minimum-copy durability gate
values.description: Require a minimum number of durable copies before acknowledging a repository write.

values.label: Synchronous replication to at least two replicas
values.description: Acknowledge a write only after synchronous commitment to at least two repository replicas.

values.label: Periodic write-ahead-log compaction
values.description: Compact accumulated WAL state periodically so restoration cost does not grow without bound.

selected_clusters.name: Repository Write Coordination
selected_clusters.description: How repository writes are ordered, replicated, attributed, and coordinated across repository-serving infrastructure.

values.label: Arbitrary replica horizontal scaling
values.description: The architecture supports deploying an arbitrary number of read-capable replicas.

values.label: Replicated compaction output
values.description: Compacted results are replicated so nodes share the same compacted representation.

values.label: External relational database for repository references
values.description: Repository references are stored in an external relational database rather than the WAL-centered design.

values.label: Globally linearized pushes
values.description: All concurrent pushes receive one globally consistent ordering.

values.label: Operation-level repository provenance
values.description: Fundamental repository operations are recorded so prior states and corruption causes can be inspected.

values.label: Orchestrator-coordinated push fan-out
values.description: Distribute pushed packs and reference transactions to repository replicas through an orchestrator.

values.label: Reference-transaction synchronization unit
values.description: Synchronize compact Git reference transactions rather than large packfiles during consensus coordination.

values.label: Consensus-free arbitrary repository primary
values.description: Allow any server to act as repository primary without elections or a fixed per-repository primary.

values.label: S3 compare-and-swap write synchronization
values.description: Synchronize concurrent write-ahead-log updates with atomic S3 compare-and-swap rather than consensus.

values.label: Cloud-agnostic object-storage deployment
values.description: Designing durable object-storage use to deploy across cloud providers rather than depend on one provider.

values.label: Single-local-repository reference synchronization
values.description: Synchronizing reference transactions with one local repository instead of a replica quorum.

values.label: Optimistic UDP replica gossip
values.description: Use lossy metadata gossip for replica notifications while replicas independently verify state and recover from durable storage.

values.label: Git compaction throughput bottleneck
values.description: After storage latency is reduced, Git compaction becomes the practical ingest limit.

selected_clusters.name: Replica Consistency and Availability Policy
selected_clusters.description: Which consistency semantics and partition-tolerance versus availability priority govern replicated repository state?

relations.reading: Choices on Replica Consistency and Availability Policy affect the outcomes of Read Replica Routing
relations.rationale: Routing can select a nearby replica only when its synchronization state and voting role satisfy the consistency policy.

values.label: Fully consistent repository replicas
values.description: All repository copies are synchronized so reads immediately observe pushed commits.

values.label: Eventually consistent repository replicas
values.description: Replicas may temporarily disagree about recently pushed commits.

values.label: Consistency and partition-tolerance priority
values.description: Prioritize consistency and partition tolerance over maximizing availability in replicated repository service.

selected_clusters.name: Consistency Enforcement and Degradation Strategy
selected_clusters.description: How is the selected consistency policy implemented and maintained during normal operation and replication or network degradation, including its operational cost?

values.label: ETag-based replica freshness verification
values.description: Check a replica's processed WAL version through conditional object-storage reads before serving repository operations.

values.label: Consistency-preserving degradation
values.description: Preserve repository correctness during replication or network degradation while using lightweight checks for healthy fast paths.

values.label: Consistency-enforcement complexity
values.description: Strong synchronization imposes substantial operational and implementation complexity.

selected_clusters.name: Replica Roles and Failure Eligibility
selected_clusters.description: Which replica roles, catch-up rules, and failure-eligibility policies govern repository participation?

values.label: Non-voting geo-replicated replicas
values.description: Geo-replicated Enterprise hosts serve reads without participating as voting push targets.

values.label: Replica rewind and fast-forward through WAL history
values.description: Replicas rewind or advance by replaying retained WAL history without an external object database.

values.label: Network-wait work overlap
values.description: Overlapping computation and local work with remote replica lock, checksum, and database operations.

values.label: Direct durable-log catch-up before reads
values.description: Replicas catch up from the authoritative WAL before serving reads when freshness metadata has advanced.

values.label: Write refusal during replication shortfall
values.description: Refuse writes when the required durable replica count cannot be reached.

values.label: Isolation of losing replicas
values.description: Remove replicas that lose a write vote from read and write eligibility until repair completes.

values.label: Temporary write unavailability under insufficient replication
values.description: Remain durable but temporarily unavailable for writes while required replica copies are missing.

selected_clusters.name: Replication Factor and Write Quorum
selected_clusters.description: Which replica count and write-quorum requirements govern durable repository updates?

values.label: Three-copy repository replication
values.description: Maintaining at least three repository replicas for availability and durability across server failures.

values.label: Majority-write replica quorum
values.description: Acknowledging writes only after a majority, including at least two replicas, commits the same state.

values.label: Distant-replica latency budget
values.description: Continental network latency consumes the available time budget for replica coordination.

values.label: Slowest-replica latency bound
values.description: Bound coordinated operation latency by the slowest participating replica.

values.label: Replica-count-induced push-throughput degradation
values.description: Adding replicas reduces push throughput when each update coordinates across the full replica set.

values.label: Monorepo traffic capacity shortfall
values.description: A fixed small replica set cannot provide sufficient serving capacity for massive monorepo traffic.

values.label: Replication overhead for repository proliferation
values.description: A mandatory replica floor creates excessive mostly idle storage and coordination for numerous small repositories.

selected_clusters.name: Replica Transaction Coordination
selected_clusters.description: How transactions are synchronized and ordered across repository replicas during replicated updates.

values.label: Three-copy quorum failure condition
values.description: Losing two of three repository copies removes quorum and blocks pushes.

values.label: Four-round-trip replica coordination
values.description: Coordinating distant replica commit and locking through four network round trips.

values.label: Three-phase commit replica synchronization
values.description: Coordinate reference updates with prepare, commit, and rollback phases across replicas.

values.label: Replica locking for update ordering
values.description: Using replicas as distributed locks to serialize database updates across the repository system.

values.label: Advanced consensus coordination
values.description: Adopting a more advanced consensus protocol to reduce distant-replica coordination round trips.

values.label: Primaryless per-write ordering
values.description: Determine each write's winning order through voting rather than following a designated primary.

values.label: Single-primary replication protocol
values.description: Use one primary replica to dictate replicated write order.

values.label: Majority-vote rollback
values.description: Revert updates on replicas where a write was applied but failed to achieve majority agreement.

selected_clusters.name: Read Replica Routing
selected_clusters.description: How Git reads are assigned across geographically distributed replicas and how write-side reference work is prioritized.

relations.reading: Read Replica Routing requires Replica Consistency and Availability Policy to be decided first
relations.rationale: A router must know which replicas are synchronized and eligible before selecting a geographically close read target.

values.label: Closest synchronized replica routing
values.description: Fetches and clones are sent to the geographically closest replica known to be up to date.

values.label: Spokes geo-replication
values.description: Spokes distributes repositories across geographic locations to support nearby Git reads.

values.label: Coalesced bookkeeping reference updates
values.description: Non-user-critical bookkeeping updates are combined into fewer transactions.

values.label: Priority scheduling for user reference updates
values.description: Latency-sensitive user updates are processed ahead of bookkeeping work.

values.label: Reduced Git transfer latency
values.description: Nearby synchronized replicas reduce fetch and clone latency.

values.label: Protection against user-request delays
values.description: Prioritization prevents bookkeeping cascades from delaying or timing out user requests.

selected_clusters.name: Filesystem-monitor implementation
selected_clusters.description: Which component provides the filesystem change-monitoring mechanism?

values.label: Watchman-backed filesystem monitoring
values.description: A filesystem-monitoring hook supplies change information without repeated broad filesystem scans.

values.label: Built-in Git filesystem monitor
values.description: Git's integrated monitor detects changed paths without an external Watchman service.

selected_clusters.name: Git-specific watcher awareness
selected_clusters.description: Does the watcher understand Git-specific directory exclusions and repository semantics?

values.label: Git-aware custom filesystem watcher
values.description: A watcher integrated with Git applies repository-specific exclusions while detecting working-tree changes.

values.label: Watchman-based filesystem watching
values.description: Use general-purpose Watchman to detect working-tree changes despite lacking Git-specific exclusion awareness.

selected_clusters.name: Repository Cache Deployment
selected_clusters.description: Whether and how a dedicated cache server supports large-repository access.

values.label: GVFS with co-located cache server
values.description: Large repositories use nearby cache infrastructure to serve GVFS requests for large user populations.

values.label: GVFS without cache-server infrastructure
values.description: GVFS is used without the infrastructure needed to handle its serving demands.

values.label: Cache-assisted transfer performance
values.description: Co-located cache proxying reduces transfer latency and central-server load while increasing throughput.

selected_clusters.name: Repository Routing Model
selected_clusters.description: Which authority and routing behavior determine where a repository is expected to be served, including how routing state handles failure or staleness?

values.label: External repository routing database
values.description: An external database maps each repository to every machine hosting a replica.

values.label: Rendezvous-hashed repository routing
values.description: Derive expected repository placement from repository identity and currently healthy nodes without durable placement state.

values.label: Tolerance of stale routing state
values.description: Allow placement hints to become stale because correctness survives by rematerializing repositories elsewhere.

values.label: Rendezvous-ranked primary selection
values.description: Normally choose the highest-ranked healthy rendezvous node to reduce retries while retaining arbitrary-primary correctness.

values.label: External database availability dependency
values.description: Replica management availability depends on the external routing database.

selected_clusters.name: Replica Placement and Repair Policy
selected_clusters.description: How are replicas distributed, counted, retired, restored, and reconstructed after infrastructure changes or failures?

values.label: Rack-diverse replica placement
values.description: Placing repository replicas in different racks to tolerate rack-wide power or networking failures.

values.label: Retiring-server removal from active replica counts
values.description: Removing retiring servers from active redundancy counts while temporarily allowing service during replacement repair.

values.label: Desired-replica-count reconciliation
values.description: Continuously restore each repository to its configured replica count after server or disk failures.

values.label: N-to-N replica reconstruction
values.description: Rebuild failed repository replicas across arbitrary surviving sources and destinations in the server cluster.

selected_clusters.name: Replica checksum maintenance strategy
selected_clusters.description: How is replica state summarized and kept comparable, and what scalability trade-offs does that impose?

values.label: Per-repository checksum tracking
values.description: Continuously updated checksums validate the health of on-disk repository copies.

values.label: Incremental replica checksum maintenance
values.description: Update replica consistency checksums from reference changes instead of rescanning all references.

values.label: Full replica checksum recomputation
values.description: Recompute the complete replica checksum after every update by scanning all reference state.

values.label: Reference-update checksum throughput constraint
values.description: Checksum computation cost limits the maximum sustainable rate of reference updates.

selected_clusters.name: Corruption response and replica repair
selected_clusters.description: How are unhealthy replicas detected, scheduled for recovery, and repaired?

values.label: Rapid corruption detection and repair scheduling
values.description: Unhealthy repositories trigger rapid detection and scheduled repair jobs.

values.label: Automatic replica repair
values.description: Repair unhealthy replicas automatically while surviving replicas continue serving repository operations.

selected_clusters.name: Replica authority and operational treatment
selected_clusters.description: What status do on-disk copies have in consistency decisions, and how are individual repository copies operationally managed?

values.label: On-disk repositories as consensus source of truth
values.description: On-disk repository copies provide the authoritative basis for replica consensus.

values.label: Pet-style repository operations
values.description: Each repository copy receives individualized operational care because it is valuable.

selected_clusters.name: Replica Failure Detection
selected_clusters.description: How infrastructure observes, attributes, and responds to replica or server failures and determines offline status.

values.label: Real-traffic failure detection
values.description: Detecting replica or server failure through failures observed during real application requests.

values.label: Heartbeat-assisted failure detection
values.description: Using heartbeats as a complementary signal alongside real application traffic for failure detection and recovery.

values.label: Three-consecutive-failure offline threshold
values.description: Demoting or marking a node offline after three consecutive failed requests.

values.label: Advisory replica demotion
values.description: Demoting suspected failed replicas in preference order without removing them from fallback availability.

values.label: RPC failover graph failure detection
values.description: Inferring server faults from the pattern of RPC operations failing over between servers.

values.label: Application-server-specific failure views
values.description: Maintaining failure observations separately at each application server rather than using one global view.

values.label: Cross-observer fault attribution
values.description: Comparing failure reports across application servers to distinguish file-server from application-server faults.

values.label: Heartbeat load polling and recovery confirmation
values.description: Using heartbeats to poll load and restore a node's online preference after failure recovery.

values.label: Heartbeat-only primary failure detection
values.description: Relying on heartbeats as the primary mechanism for detecting failed nodes.

values.label: MxN failure-detector topology
values.description: Have each application server independently monitor each repository server through RPCs and heartbeats.

values.label: Heartbeat detection delay
values.description: Delayed awareness of failures when periodic heartbeats lag behind failures observed in live traffic.

values.label: Synthetic health-check functional blind spots
values.description: No-op health checks can miss failures in Git execution, disks, or authenticated operations.

values.label: False offline marking from consecutive request failures
values.description: A healthy node can be temporarily marked offline after unrelated request failures happen consecutively.

values.label: Localized failure-detector errors
values.description: Keep an observer's mistaken offline view local rather than allowing it to determine system-wide server status.

selected_clusters.name: Git Hosting Collaboration Model
selected_clusters.description: Whether repository collaboration is organized around decentralized copies or centralized hosting.

values.label: Decentralized maintainer workflow
values.description: Many subsystem maintainers collaborate through decentralized repository ownership and exchange.

values.label: Centralized repository hosting
values.description: Teams use a central host while retaining distributed-client capabilities.

values.label: Offline local work
values.description: Developers can continue repository work without network connectivity.

values.label: Delayed push workflow
values.description: Developers can postpone transmitting local changes to the host.

values.label: Distributed version-control architecture
values.description: Repository collaboration preserves distributed copies and decentralized exchange.

values.label: Distributed architecture as a hindrance for centralized workflows
values.description: Distributed design can hinder projects whose collaboration is primarily centralized.

values.label: Large-scale Git hosting difficulty
values.description: Hosting Git repositories at scale creates exceptional operational difficulty.

selected_clusters.name: Server Maintenance Operations
selected_clusters.description: How hosting servers are tested, quiesced, rebooted, and retired without disrupting repository reads.

values.label: Rolling reboot testing
values.description: Servers are rebooted in controlled sequence after quiescing outstanding reads.

values.label: Chaos-monkey testing on file servers
values.description: Random server reboots are used as a failure-testing approach.

values.label: Unplanned server unplugging for retirement
values.description: A server is abruptly disconnected without quiescence or redundancy planning.

values.label: Crash-like mechanisms for planned maintenance
values.description: Planned reboots and retirement reuse crash or permanent-failure handling for transparent replica failover.

values.label: Server quiescing before reboot
values.description: Withdraw a server from new reads, drain existing reads, and keep replication active before shutdown.

values.label: Direct server reboot for planned maintenance
values.description: Reboot a server directly without quiescing or draining work first.

values.label: Two-copy repository state after sudden server loss
values.description: Sudden server loss temporarily leaves repositories with two readable but less resilient copies.

values.label: Increased same-day write-rejection risk
values.description: Sudden server removal increases the likelihood that later writes will be rejected.

values.label: Lost progress from interrupted long-running reads
values.description: Abrupt maintenance interrupts lengthy reads and forces them to restart elsewhere.

values.label: Replica catch-up load from withheld writes
values.description: Stopping writes during quiescing creates replica lag and catch-up work after return.

selected_clusters.name: Client Working-Tree Scope
selected_clusters.description: How much repository content is materialized in the client working tree.

values.label: Sparse working-tree population
values.description: Materialize only selected repository paths by default, expanding populated directories on demand.

values.label: Full working-tree population
values.description: Materialize all tracked repository files through an explicit full-clone override.

values.label: Populated-file modification-detection cost
values.description: Reduced populated-file scope lowers the cost of detecting modifications in client working trees.

selected_clusters.name: Client capability ownership and migration
selected_clusters.description: Where should large-repository performance capabilities reside, and what migration relationship should exist between a management layer and core Git?

values.label: Scalar performance layer
values.description: A management layer temporarily supplies large-repository performance capabilities.

values.label: Core Git capability investment
values.description: Performance capabilities are implemented directly in the core Git client.

values.label: Transition from Scalar to core Git
values.description: Clients progressively eliminate the management layer as core Git gains equivalent capabilities.

selected_clusters.name: Capability improvement and delivery approach
selected_clusters.description: How should large-repository capabilities be identified, improved, and distributed to clients?

values.label: Feedback-driven performance optimization
values.description: Use tracing and user feedback to identify and address client Git performance bottlenecks.

values.label: Custom Git distribution
values.description: Ship large-repository capabilities in a customized Git distribution while extending availability to other Git forks.

selected_clusters.name: Client Repository Directory Layout
selected_clusters.description: How client repository source trees and generated build outputs are arranged on disk.

values.label: Nested source working directory
values.description: Place the working directory below the repository root to leave room for sibling build outputs.

values.label: Sibling build-output directories
values.description: Keep generated build artifacts outside the Git-managed working directory in sibling directories.

selected_clusters.name: Client Materialization and Metadata
selected_clusters.description: Which client-side materialization and metadata mechanisms scale operations for very large repositories and working trees.

values.label: Updated Git index format
values.description: Use a more compact index representation for repositories with millions of tracked paths.

values.label: Untracked cache
values.description: Maintain cached untracked-path metadata to reduce repeated working-directory scans in large repositories.

values.label: Complete tracked-path index
values.description: Represent every tracked path at the current HEAD in the client index.

values.label: Single-file index storage
values.description: Store the client index as one file read and written by core Git commands.

values.label: Disabled ahead-behind calculation
values.description: Status avoids repeated ahead-behind comparison work during routine status operations.

values.label: Sparse checkout for reduced working trees
values.description: Only selected paths are materialized in the working directory.

values.label: Compressed client index size
values.description: Reduce the physical size and I/O volume of the client index file.

criteria.name: Orthogonality
criteria.description: Every dimension is a distinct decision point: no two dimensions ask the same question, and no dimension's candidate decisions are really options of another dimension.
criteria.reason: Several dimensions ask substantially overlapping questions. Dimension 22, "Repository Replication Granularity," and dimension 47, "Replication layer," both decide the layer or unit at which repository state is replicated; merge them and retain their alternatives under one question. Dimensions 34, "Client Pack Rewrite Strategy," and 54, "Client Object-Cleanup Pipeline," also overlap around repacking, replacement packs, and pack expiration; merge or reorganize them so one dimension asks about rewrite strategy and the other, if retained, asks only about object-cleanup scope. Dimensions 38, "Replica Allocation and Lifecycle," and 58, "Replica Placement and Repair Policy," both cover replica counts, retirement, reconstruction, and recovery; merge them or move the shared lifecycle values into one dimension. Dimension 15, "Client Working-Tree Scope," duplicates the "Sparse checkout for reduced working trees" value in dimension 32; move value 32.6 to dimension 15 because it answers the materialization-scope question. Dimension 55, "Replica Compaction Strategy," overlaps with dimension 34's compaction/repacking alternatives and should be narrowed or reorganized so compaction location/distribution is distinct from pack-rewrite mechanics. Other pairs such as 61/62 and 25/26 ask different policy versus implementation questions and should not be merged.

criteria.name: Clarity
criteria.description: Dimension names and descriptions make the decision question clear, and value labels and descriptions make the alternatives distinguishable, so a reader could tell which dimension and value a passage about a design decision belongs to.
criteria.reason: Most dimensions state explicit questions and most values have concrete, distinguishable descriptions, such as 42's foreground versus background maintenance and 57's database versus rendezvous routing. However, value 51.1 and rejected value 51.3 both describe essentially the same virtualized-filesystem approach; merge them or rewrite them to identify a concrete alternative. Value 40.3, "Network-wait work overlap," does not match dimension 40's replica-role, catch-up, and failure-eligibility question; move it to a coordination or performance dimension. Dimension 33 also contains broad, non-alternative entries such as 33.3 "Hosted version-control platform" and 33.4 "Continual hosting-platform evolution" whose descriptions do not clearly identify architectural choices; rename or reorganize that dimension so each value answers the same hosting-architecture question.

criteria.name: Completeness
criteria.description: The taxonomy contains the major decision points implied by the use case, each with its main candidate decisions.
criteria.reason: The taxonomy covers the main decision areas for scaling Git across servers and clients, with multiple candidate decisions in each: client maintenance and large-repository access (42, 50, 51), client storage and metadata (34, 35, 32), server storage and durable writes (11, 25), replication and coordination (22, 26, 28, 41), consistency and routing (61, 62, 7, 57), and failure recovery and placement (31, 40, 45, 58). These dimensions generally provide accepted, rejected, or mixed alternatives rather than only single candidates, so no major coverage shortcoming is evident under the stated criterion.

criteria.name: Use case alignment
criteria.description: Every dimension serves the stated use case; none is out of its scope.
criteria.reason: Most dimensions directly address scaling Git repositories across clients, hosting servers, replicas, storage, consistency, routing, maintenance, and large-repository access, matching the use case's server/client and repository/user scale scope. The main tangential dimensions are 13, "Git Hosting Collaboration Model," which focuses on collaboration philosophy and offline workflows rather than scaling architecture; 17, "Client Repository Directory Layout," which concerns source/build-directory organization rather than repository scalability; and 53, "Capability improvement and delivery approach," which concerns feedback and distribution processes rather than architectural decisions. Drop those dimensions, or move their architecture-relevant content into existing client or hosting dimensions.

criteria.reason: Most dimensions and values are specific decisions or outcomes, with no literal 'Other' or 'Miscellaneous' buckets. The main catch-all is dimension 33, "Hosting Application Architecture", which bundles deployment structure, platform identity, evolution, optimization, and migration; split it into existing-content questions for application deployment/scaling (33.1–33.2) and platform evolution/migration (33.3–33.4, 33.6), and drop or reclassify the generic value 33.5, "Reliability, performance, and scale optimization." Value 13.5, "Distributed version-control architecture," is also a broad summary rather than a distinct alternative; drop it or merge its content into 13.1, "Decentralized maintainer workflow."

criteria.name: Axis vs. value
criteria.description: Each dimension is a decision point with alternatives, not a single option presented as a dimension; each value is an option, not a sub-topic.
criteria.reason: The output contains some valid single decisions, such as 42 (Client Maintenance Execution Mode), but many dimensions bundle multiple independent decisions. Dimension 25 (Durable Repository Write Storage) mixes WAL architecture, object-storage backend, batching, acknowledgement gates, replication durability, and compaction; reorganize its existing values into separate one-question dimensions. Dimension 26 (Repository Write Coordination) similarly combines scaling, ordering, provenance, fan-out, primary selection, synchronization, and gossip; split or relocate those value groups so each dimension represents one decision. Dimension 31 (Replica Failure Detection) combines detection signals, thresholds, observer topology, fault attribution, and recovery behavior; separate these decision questions using its existing values. Dimension 32 (Client Materialization and Metadata) mixes index representation, untracked-cache behavior, status calculation, sparse checkout, and outcomes; separate the mechanisms into appropriate existing client-maintenance decisions. Dimension 57 (Repository Routing Model) combines routing authority, hashing algorithm, stale-state tolerance, primary selection, and an availability outcome; split these into distinct decisions and move 57.5 out as an outcome rather than treating all of them as alternatives to one question.

criteria.reason: Many dimensions have at least two candidate decisions, but numerous broad topics combine different decision questions, substantially violating the taxonomy requirement. Dimension 25 (Durable Repository Write Storage) mixes WAL backend, batching, acknowledgement/quorum, and compaction choices; split these into separate decision points and move each value to the question it answers. Dimension 26 (Repository Write Coordination) similarly combines ordering, dissemination, consensus, primary selection, synchronization, and deployment concerns and should be split. Dimension 11 (Repository Physical Storage) mixes physical medium, hosting location, co-location, and cache/authority semantics; separate those questions. Dimension 31 (Replica Failure Detection) combines detection signals, thresholds, observer scope, attribution, and failover treatment; split the mechanisms from policy and response. Dimension 32 (Client Materialization and Metadata) mixes index representation, metadata caching, status behavior, and working-tree materialization; move value 32.6 to dimension 15 and split the remaining index/metadata choices. These broad groupings are especially problematic for the use case's separate client, server, repository-scale, and user-scale decisions, even though several smaller dimensions such as 42, 47, 59, 60, and 15 are well formed.
